outcomes.title: [AI DRAFT] Explain a function from the workspace
outcomes.prose:
**What it does:** `debounce(fn, wait)` returns a wrapped version of `fn`. Each call to the wrapper cancels any pending timer and starts a new `wait` ms timer. `fn` runs only after `wait` ms pass with no new calls, and it receives the arguments from the last call.

Limitations of this version:
- It is trailing-edge only, so there is no immediate first call.
- There is no `cancel` or `flush`.
- `this` isn't preserved, because the wrapper is an arrow function.
- The return value of `fn` is discarded.

**Debounce vs. throttle:**
- **Debounce** waits for a burst of events to stop and then fires once. Use it when only the final state matters:
  - search-as-you-type requests
  - validating a form after the user pauses
  - saving a draft after editing stops
  - recalculating layout after a window resize ends
- **Throttle** fires at most once per interval while events keep coming. Use it when you need regular updates during continuous activity:
  - scroll position tracking
  - drag or mousemove handlers
  - progress reporting
  - rate-limiting button spam

A debounced function never fires while events keep arriving, so a continuous stream starves it. If you need periodic updates during that stream, use throttle.

outcomes.title: [AI DRAFT] Design-language persona: developer, benchmark takeaway

components.text: ## simdjson-port is fastest at every size, and its lead grows with input

components.title: Caveats
components.text: Gains at 1 KB are tiny in absolute terms (0.05 ms). v2 and serde-wasm are roughly equal. Check variance, memory use, and bundle size before deciding; medians alone hide them.

outcomes.prose:
Takeaways:

- **simdjson-port wins at every size.** Its speedup over v1 grows from about 2.7× at 1 KB to about 7.7× at 10 MB, so it matters most for large payloads.
- **v2 is only about 2× faster than v1.** That's a steady gain, but it flattens out at larger sizes.
- **serde-wasm is slightly ahead of v2 on mid and large inputs.** It's about 7% faster at 100 KB and 11% at 10 MB. At 1 KB it's slightly slower (0.06 vs 0.05 ms).
- **Small inputs barely matter.** The differences at 1 KB are tens of microseconds, so call overhead will probably swamp them.

If your workloads are mostly large, adopt simdjson-port. Before committing, check its memory use, its correctness on edge cases, and any portability or build costs. These benchmarks are medians only, so they don't show variance.

components.text: ## You don't run out in any of the three cases
Revenue reaches the $38k monthly spend in month 24 at 5%, month 15 at 8% and month 11 at 12%. After that the business is cash-flow positive.

components.title: Assumption
components.text: I treated $38k as total monthly spend, so net burn is $38k minus revenue. If $38k is already net of revenue, runway is just 480/38 ≈ 12.6 months, with no growth effect.

outcomes.prose:
You don't run out of money in any of the three cases. That holds only if the $38k a month is your total spend, with revenue coming in on top of it. The figures are in the view above.

Cash falls until revenue catches up with spend, then it recovers. The 5% case is the tightest, with about $102k left at its lowest point in month 24.

If the $38k is already net of revenue, the answer is different. Cash would run out in about 12.6 months, and growth would make no difference.
